h1: Amps to Watts Calculator (DC, AC and 3-Phase)
author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: amps
fields.label: Current
fields.hint: Amps from a clamp meter, the appliance label, or the breaker or socket rating you want to check.

fields.name: mode
fields.label: Supply type
fields.hint: For three-phase enter the current in one line wire; the calculator adds the other two.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Voltage
fields.hint: Leave blank for standard mains: 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase line to line. For DC enter the battery voltage; for the US enter 120.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor
fields.hint: 1 for heaters and other resistive loads; about 0.8 for motors, ACs and mixed home loads. Ignored for DC.

answer: {{in.amps|int}} amps on a {{in.volts|int}} V single-phase supply is {{out.watts|int}} watts at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}, and {{out.va|int}} W for a heater with a power factor of one. Watts = amps × volts × power factor; DC uses a power factor of one, and three-phase multiplies by the square root of three.
how: {{out.k|4}} × {{in.amps}} A × {{out.volts}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor = {{out.watts|int}} W ({{out.kw|2}} kW). The first factor is one for DC and single-phase and √3 for three-phase, where the volts are line-to-line and the amps are per line. Without the power factor the result is {{out.va|int}} VA, the apparent power the wires carry. On DC the power factor is one.
key_facts: Watts = amps × volts × power factor. {{in.amps|int}} A at {{in.volts|int}} V and a power factor of {{out.pf|2}} is {{out.watts|int}} W, out of {{out.va|int}} VA of apparent power.
One amp on a {{ex.0.out.volts|int}} V supply carries {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W of heating load; on a {{ex.3.out.volts|int}} V battery one amp carries only {{ex.3.out.volts|int}} W.
A {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A circuit at {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V (common in the US) carries at most {{ex.2.out.watts|int}} W of heating load before the breaker's rating is reached.
On three-phase, {{ex.4.in.amps|int}} A per line at {{ex.4.out.volts|int}} V and a power factor of {{ex.4.in.pf|2}} is {{ex.4.out.watts|int}} W, because three lines share the load.

formula.text: DC: P = V × I;  single-phase AC: P = V × I × PF;  three-phase AC: P = √3 × V × I × PF
lines: P = real power in watts (W); kW = W ÷ 1,000
I = current in amps (A), per line for three-phase
V = voltage: battery voltage for DC, phase-to-neutral for single-phase, line-to-line for three-phase
PF = power factor between 0 and 1; V × I without PF is the apparent power in VA

sections.h2: One amp is how many watts?
p: It depends on the voltage. On {{ex.0.out.volts|int}} V mains with a heating load, one amp is {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W. On a {{ex.3.out.volts|int}} V battery, one amp is just {{ex.3.out.volts|int}} W. For motors and ACs, multiply by the power factor as well, so one amp delivers less real power than the volts suggest.

sections.h2: How many watts can a circuit or breaker handle?
p: Multiply the breaker's amps by the voltage. A {{in.amps|int}} A circuit on {{in.volts|int}} V carries {{out.va|int}} VA, which is {{out.va|int}} W of heaters but only {{out.watts|int}} W of motors and ACs at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}. The chart below lists the common breaker sizes.

That figure is the ceiling, not a target. A load that runs for hours should stay well under it: the wiring calculators on this site size cables at {{d.margin|2}} times the running current, and starting surges of motors and compressors come on top.

Choose three-phase and enter the current in one line. The calculator uses the line-to-line voltage ({{d.v_3ph|int}} V in Pakistan) and the square root of three: {{ex.4.in.amps|int}} A per line at a power factor of {{ex.4.in.pf|2}} is {{ex.4.out.watts|int}} W. If you know the kW and need the current, the 3 phase amps calculator works the other way.

sections.h2: Watts versus VA: why there are two answers
p: Volts × amps gives volt-amperes (VA), the apparent power the cable and breaker carry. Real watts are VA × power factor, the power that turns into heat, light or motion and that the meter counts. For a heater both are equal; for a motor the watts are lower. UPS and generator ratings in VA or kVA follow the same rule.

examples.title: {{in.amps|int}} amp at {{out.volts|int}} V: how many watts?
examples.text: {{in.amps|int}} A × {{out.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}} = {{out.watts|int}} W for a heating load. With a power factor below one, the same amp carries fewer real watts.

examples.title: {{in.amps|int}} amps to watts at {{out.volts|int}} V
examples.text: {{in.amps|int}} A × {{out.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}} = {{out.watts|int}} W ({{out.kw|2}} kW). That is roughly one large room heater or a kettle and an iron together.

examples.title: How many watts can a {{in.amps|int}} A circuit at {{in.volts|int}} V handle?
examples.text: {{in.amps|int}} A × {{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}} = {{out.watts|int}} W at most for heating loads. Long-running loads should stay well below this so the cable and breaker do not run at their limit.

examples.title: {{in.amps|int}} amps from a {{in.volts|int}} V battery
examples.text: {{in.amps|int}} A × {{in.volts|int}} V = {{out.watts|int}} W. DC has no power factor, so the watts are simply volts times amps.

examples.title: {{in.amps|int}} amps per line on three-phase {{out.volts|int}} V
examples.text: √3 × {{out.volts|int}} V × {{in.amps|int}} A × {{in.pf|2}} = {{out.watts|int}} W ({{out.kw|2}} kW). The apparent power is {{out.va|int}} VA.

mistakes: Multiplying amps by volts for a motor or AC and calling it watts. That is VA; the real watts are lower by the power factor (about {{d.pf_mixed|2}}).
Loading a circuit right up to the watts in the chart. Those are ceilings; a heater or AC running for hours should leave a margin, and motors surge above their running current at start-up.
Using {{d.v_1ph|int}} V with the three-phase formula. Three-phase uses the line-to-line voltage ({{d.v_3ph|int}} V) and the square root of three, with the current of one line.
Copying a US chart for a {{d.v_1ph|int}} V supply. The same amps carry about twice the watts at {{d.v_1ph|int}} V as at {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V, so always use the voltage of your own supply.
safety: The watts a breaker allows are a ceiling for the circuit, not permission to add loads. Before putting a heater, AC or motor on an existing circuit, check the cable size with the wire size calculator and have a licensed electrician confirm the circuit.

faq.a: {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W on a {{ex.0.out.volts|int}} V supply with a heating load. With a power factor of {{d.pf_mixed|2}} (motors, mixed loads) it is less, and on a {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V battery one amp is only {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} W.
{{ex.1.out.watts|int}} W at {{ex.1.out.volts|int}} V with a power factor of one, or {{ex.1.out.kw|2}} kW.

faq.q: How many watts is {{in.amps|int}} A at {{in.volts|int}} V?
faq.a: {{out.va|int}} W for heating loads and {{out.watts|int}} W at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}. A {{in.amps|int}} A socket circuit can carry one large heater or AC, but not several at once.

faq.q: How many watts can a {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} amp circuit handle?
faq.a: At {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V the ceiling is {{ex.2.out.watts|int}} W for heating loads. Loads that run for hours should stay well below it, and motors and ACs need room for their starting surge.

faq.q: What is the amps to watts formula?
faq.a: Watts = volts × amps for DC; watts = volts × amps × power factor for single-phase AC; watts = √3 × line-to-line volts × amps × power factor for three-phase.

faq.q: How do I convert amps to watts on three-phase?
faq.a: Multiply √3 × line-to-line volts × the current in one line × power factor. {{ex.4.in.amps|int}} A per line at {{ex.4.out.volts|int}} V and a power factor of {{ex.4.in.pf|2}} is {{ex.4.out.watts|int}} W.

faq.q: How many watts is {{ex.3.in.amps|int}} amps at {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V DC?
faq.a: {{ex.3.out.watts|int}} W. On DC the watts are simply volts × amps, with no power factor.
